parole.testo: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin cantiōnem f (accusative singular), modified from the original Old Spanish cançón f, which was directly inherited, based on -ción. Compare Portuguese canção f, Catalan cançó f, French chanson f, Italian canzone f. Doublet of chanson m. Compare English cantor.
Borrowed from Latin extendere, or modified from the Old Spanish estender, which may have been inherited.

Inherited from Old Spanish gouernaçion, governaçion, from Latin gubernātiōnem (“direction, management, government”), or based on Old Spanish gouernar (“to govern”). Analytically from gobernar (“to govern”) + -ción.

parole.significato: the soft part of an animal's body; flesh
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin pŭlpa, perhaps via an unattested Old Spanish *pupa, with /l/ restored by Latin influence or contact with forms like Portuguese polpa. Compare the evolution of Spanish dulce < duce < dŭlcem.

Inherited from Old Spanish rabdo, from Latin rapidus (“swift”), via voicing of intervocalic /p/ to /b/, syncope of the following vowel, and vocalization of coda /b/ to /u̯/. Cf. the evolution of Latin cubitum > Old Spanish cobdo > modern codo, where the /u̯/ was absorbed into the preceding rounded v

From older sujuzgar, from Old Spanish sujudgar, from Latin subiugāre, and influenced by the verb juzgar (“to judge”), from Old Spanish judgar, from Latin iūdicāre. Compare the borrowed doublet subyugar.

Inherited from Latin subrīsus, perfect passive participle of subrīdeō. Less likely, according to RAE, from Old Spanish sonrisar. First attested before 1409 in a poem by Francisco Imperial (who likely died that year or before) in Cancionero de Baena.
From Latin vādāmus, the present subjunctive form, replacing Old Spanish imos in the indicative. Compare the analogical form, vayamos, which is the Spanish present subjunctive form.
